decks.title: Diversity in the Animal Kingdom — Part 1: Non-chordates
goals: State how chordates differ from non-chordates
Describe the main features and examples of the eight non-chordate phyla
Classify a given non-chordate into its phylum with reasons

slides.heading: Sorting the Animal Kingdom
slides.body_md: Part 1 — the first big split: animals without a notochord.

visual.alt: Flow from the animal kingdom to the non-chordates and the chordates

slides.narration: Millions of kinds of animals share our planet. To study them, biologists sort them into groups by their body features. The first big split is between animals with a notochord and animals without one.

slides.heading: Two big groups
slides.body_md: The kingdom **Animalia** is divided into **non-chordates** (eight phyla in this course) and **chordates**.

slides.narration: Here is the whole plan. Non-chordates are split into eight phyla, from sponges to starfish. Chordates, which include all vertebrates, are split into five classes, from fishes to mammals.

slides.heading: Chordates and non-chordates

visual.alt: Table comparing non-chordates and chordates by notochord, nerve cord, gill slits and heart

slides.narration: A notochord is a stiff rod along the back that supports the body. Chordates have it, at least when young, along with a hollow nerve cord on the back and gill slits. Non-chordates have none of these.

slides.body_md: Which feature is found only in chordates?
slides.narration: Think of the rod along the back.

slides.heading: Sponges and Hydra
slides.body_md: A sponge is full of **pores**; a Hydra has **tentacles** with **stinging cells**.

slides.heading: Porifera and Coelenterata

rows: Many pores and one large opening, the osculum
Tube-shaped, with tentacles around the mouth
Soft body, no skeleton in Hydra

visual.alt: Table comparing sponges and coelenterates by body, special cells, support and examples

slides.narration: Sponges are pore bearers, which is what the name Porifera means. Coelenterates catch their prey with stinging cells on the tentacles, and a single opening serves as both mouth and anus.

slides.body_md: What are the stinging cells of a Hydra called?
slides.narration: The tentacles carry them.

slides.heading: Three kinds of body cavity
slides.body_md: Worm-like animals differ in their **body cavity**: **none**, a **false cavity** or a **true cavity (coelom)**.

slides.heading: The three worm phyla

visual.alt: Table comparing flatworms, roundworms and segmented worms by shape, body cavity and examples

slides.narration: Flatworms are flat and have no body cavity. Roundworms are round, with a false cavity. Annelids have a body divided into rings and a true cavity. Many flatworms and roundworms are parasites.

slides.narration: Think of the round, unsegmented worms.

slides.body_md: A **mollusc** has a **soft body**, often with a **shell** and a **muscular foot**. An **echinoderm** has **spiny skin** and **tube feet**.

slides.narration: A snail is a mollusc. Its soft body is protected by a shell, and it creeps on a muscular foot. A starfish is an echinoderm. Its skin is spiny, and it moves on tube feet along its five arms.

slides.heading: Arthropoda, Mollusca, Echinodermata

rows: Jointed legs; hard outer skeleton; body in segments
Soft unsegmented body; mantle; usually a shell; muscular foot
Spiny skin; tube feet; five-part body in adults; all marine

visual.alt: Table of the key features and examples of Arthropoda, Mollusca and Echinodermata

slides.narration: Remember one clue for each phylum. Jointed legs mean arthropod. A soft body with a foot and often a shell means mollusc. Spiny skin with tube feet means echinoderm. Octopus and cuttlefish are molluscs even though they have no outer shell.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: counting legs
slides.body_md: A jar holds 7 insects and 3 spiders. Insects have 6 legs and spiders have 8 legs. How many legs are there in all?
bullets: Step 1: insect legs = 7 × 6 = **42**.
Step 2: spider legs = 3 × 8 = **24**.
Step 3: total = 42 + 24 = **66**. Both animals have jointed legs, so both belong to **Arthropoda**.

visual.alt: Worked table of legs counted in a jar of insects and spiders

slides.narration: Work out the legs for each animal first, then add them. Seven insects with six legs each give forty two legs. Three spiders with eight legs each give twenty four. That makes sixty six legs, and all of these animals are arthropods.

slides.heading: Quick check: jointed legs
slides.body_md: Which phylum has jointed legs and a hard outer skeleton?
slides.narration: The name means jointed feet.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a survey tally
slides.body_md: A class collected 40 animals on a shore and a pond: 16 arthropods, 10 molluscs, 6 echinoderms, 4 annelids and 4 coelenterates. What percentage were arthropods, and how many were molluscs or annelids?
bullets: Step 1: percentage of arthropods = 16 ÷ 40 × 100 = **40 percent**.
Step 2: molluscs and annelids together = 10 + 4 = **14**.

visual.alt: Worked table of a survey of forty animals by phylum with the percentage in each

slides.narration: Divide the number in one group by the total and multiply by one hundred. Sixteen out of forty is forty percent. For molluscs and annelids together, simply add the two counts, which gives fourteen.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Chordates have a notochord, a hollow nerve cord on the back and gill slits; non-chordates have none of these.
Porifera: pores. Coelenterata: tentacles and stinging cells.
Worms: flat (no cavity), round (false cavity), ringed (true cavity).
Arthropoda: jointed legs. Mollusca: soft body and foot. Echinodermata: spiny skin and tube feet.

visual.alt: Summary table of one clue for each of the eight non-chordate phyla

slides.narration: To recap. Learn one clue for each phylum: pores, stinging cells, flat body, round body, rings, jointed legs, soft body with a foot, and spiny skin with tube feet.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Always give the **phylum name** and at least **one feature** as the reason.
Spell the phyla correctly: **Nemathelminthes**, **Platyhelminthes**, **Coelenterata**.
Octopus and cuttlefish are **molluscs**; a spider is an **arthropod**, not an insect.
In a labelled diagram, draw **ruled lines** that touch the part.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Name the phylum and give one feature as your reason. Spell the phylum names carefully. Remember that an octopus is a mollusc and that a spider is an arthropod but not an insect. Label diagrams with ruled lines.

decks.title: Diversity in the Animal Kingdom — Part 2: Chordates
goals: State the distinguishing features of the five classes of vertebrates
Classify a given vertebrate into its class with reasons

slides.heading: The Chordates
slides.body_md: Part 2 — animals with a notochord, and their five classes.

visual.alt: Flow listing the five classes of chordates in order: Pisces, Amphibia, Reptilia, Aves and Mammalia

slides.narration: The chordates in this course are all vertebrates, animals with a backbone. They are divided into five classes: fishes, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals.

slides.heading: What makes a chordate

rows: A stiff supporting rod along the back, replaced by the backbone in vertebrates
The spinal cord, lying along the back
Slits in the throat, at least in the embryo
Heart on the belly side; a tail behind the anus at some stage

visual.alt: Table of the features of chordates

slides.narration: Chordates share three key features. A notochord along the back, a hollow nerve cord above it, and gill slits in the throat. In vertebrates the notochord is replaced by the backbone as the animal grows.

slides.heading: Pisces and Amphibia

rows: Skin and lungs; gills in the young

visual.alt: Table comparing fishes and amphibians by habitat, skin, breathing, heart and examples

slides.narration: Fishes live in water, breathe with gills, have scales and fins, and a two chambered heart. Amphibians live both on land and in water, with moist skin and a three chambered heart. The young breathe with gills and change into adults by metamorphosis.

slides.heading: Quick check: moist skin
slides.body_md: Which class has a moist skin without scales and a larva that has gills?
slides.narration: The young change shape as they grow.

slides.heading: Reptilia, Aves and Mammalia

rows: Four short legs, or none in snakes
Limbs for walking, flying or swimming

visual.alt: Table comparing reptiles, birds and mammals by body covering, limbs, heart, body temperature, young and examples

slides.narration: Reptiles have dry scales and lay shelled eggs on land. Birds have feathers, wings and a beak. Mammals have hair and feed their young on milk from mammary glands. Birds and mammals are warm blooded.

slides.heading: Heart chambers
slides.body_md: The number of **heart chambers** rises from **two** in fishes to **four** in birds and mammals.

slides.narration: Look at how the heart changes. Fishes have one atrium and one ventricle. Amphibians and reptiles have two atria and one ventricle. Birds and mammals have two atria and two ventricles, which keeps oxygen rich blood separate.

slides.heading: Quick check: four chambers
slides.body_md: Which pair of classes has a four-chambered heart?
slides.narration: Both are warm blooded.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: which class?
slides.body_md: An animal has dry scaly skin, four short legs, lungs, a three-chambered heart and lays leathery-shelled eggs on land. Which class is it?
bullets: Step 1: list the clues: **dry scales**, **three-chambered heart**, **eggs with a shell on land**.
Step 2: scales rule out amphibians (moist skin) and mammals (hair); the heart rules out birds and mammals.
Step 3: only **Reptilia** fits all the clues. A lizard is an example.

visual.alt: Worked table showing how three clues are used to decide that an animal is a reptile

slides.narration: Use each clue to cross out classes. Dry scaly skin removes amphibians. A three chambered heart removes birds and mammals. Shelled eggs laid on land remove fishes. Only reptiles fit all the clues.

slides.heading: Comparing the five classes

visual.alt: Table of heart chambers, body temperature and breathing organ in the five vertebrate classes

slides.narration: Compare the five classes side by side. Only birds and mammals are warm blooded, and only they have four heart chambers. Fishes breathe with gills, while reptiles, birds and mammals all breathe with lungs.

slides.heading: Quick check: a flying mammal
slides.body_md: Why is a bat placed in the class Mammalia although it flies?
slides.narration: Think of hair and milk.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a museum shelf
slides.body_md: A shelf holds 30 vertebrate specimens: 9 fishes, 6 amphibians, 7 reptiles, 5 birds and 3 mammals. How many are warm-blooded, and what percentage are cold-blooded?
bullets: Step 1: warm-blooded = birds + mammals = 5 + 3 = **8**.
Step 2: cold-blooded = 9 + 6 + 7 = **22**.
Step 3: percentage cold-blooded = 22 ÷ 30 × 100 = **73.3 percent**.

visual.alt: Worked table of cold-blooded and warm-blooded specimens on a shelf of thirty

slides.narration: Sort the classes into warm blooded and cold blooded first. Birds and mammals are the warm blooded ones, so five plus three gives eight. The other twenty two are cold blooded, which is seventy three point three percent of thirty.

slides.heading: A key to the classes
slides.body_md: Ask questions in order to reach the class.

visual.alt: Flow chart of questions that leads to one of the five vertebrate classes

slides.narration: A key works by asking one question at a time. Gills and fins mean fish. Moist skin with a gilled young stage means amphibian. Feathers mean bird. Hair and milk glands mean mammal. Dry scales without these other signs mean reptile.

slides.heading: Quick check: dry scaly skin
slides.body_md: Which class lays shelled eggs on land and has dry, scaly skin?
slides.narration: Think of a lizard.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Chordates: notochord, hollow nerve cord on the back, gill slits.
Pisces: gills, scales, two chambers. Amphibia: moist skin, metamorphosis, three chambers.
Reptilia: dry scales, shelled eggs on land. Aves: feathers, wings, four chambers. Mammalia: hair, milk glands, four chambers.
Only birds and mammals are warm-blooded.

visual.alt: Summary table of the five classes with an example and one clue each

slides.narration: To recap. Fishes have gills and scales. Amphibians have moist skin and metamorphosis. Reptiles have dry scales. Birds have feathers, and mammals have hair and milk glands. Birds and mammals are warm blooded.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Support every class with **two or more features** and an **example**.
A **bat** is a mammal, a **whale** is a mammal, a **penguin** is a bird.
Write **metamorphosis** for amphibians; **warm-blooded** for birds and mammals.
Compare in a **table** when the question says differences.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Give two or more features and an example for each class. Remember that bats and whales are mammals and penguins are birds. Use the word metamorphosis for amphibians. Write differences in a table, point by point.

notes.title: Diversity in the Animal Kingdom — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Kingdom Animalia: non-chordates and chordates
sections.body_md:
Animals are grouped by shared body features. The first split is on the **notochord**, a stiff rod running along the back.

| Feature | Non-chordates | Chordates |
|---|---|---|
| Notochord | Absent | Present at some stage of life |
| Nerve cord | Solid, on the belly side | Hollow, on the back (dorsal) side |
| Pharyngeal gill slits | Absent | Present at some stage (often only in the embryo) |
| Heart | On the back side, when present | On the belly side |

**Non-chordates** in this course form eight phyla: Porifera, Coelenterata, Platyhelminthes, Nemathelminthes, Annelida, Arthropoda, Mollusca and Echinodermata. **Chordates** here are the five classes of **vertebrates** (animals with a backbone): Pisces, Amphibia, Reptilia, Aves and Mammalia.

key_terms.definition_md: A stiff supporting rod along the back of a chordate; in vertebrates it is replaced by the backbone.
A major group of animals sharing a basic body plan.

sections.heading: 2. Porifera and Coelenterata
sections.body_md:
**Porifera (sponges)** — "pore bearers".
- Mostly **marine**; **fixed** to a rock or shell and do not move about.
- Body is full of **pores**; water enters through the pores and leaves through a large opening, the **osculum**; the central cavity is lined with collar-bearing cells that capture food.
- Supported by **spicules** or fibres. Examples: **Sycon**, **Spongilla** (freshwater), **Euspongia** (bath sponge).

**Coelenterata** — aquatic, mostly marine.
- Body is a **tube with two cell layers** and a central cavity (the coelenteron); a **single opening** serves as mouth and anus.
- **Tentacles** around the mouth carry **stinging cells (cnidoblasts)** used to catch prey and for defence.
- Examples: **Hydra** (freshwater), **jellyfish**, **sea anemone**, **coral**.

key_terms.definition_md: The large opening at the top of a sponge through which water leaves.
A tiny rod-like skeletal piece in the body wall of a sponge.
A stinging cell on the tentacles of a coelenterate.

sections.heading: 3. Platyhelminthes, Nemathelminthes and Annelida
sections.body_md:
| Phylum | Body | Body cavity | Other features | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Platyhelminthes** | Flat, leaf-like or ribbon-like | **None** (solid tissue) | Many are **parasites** with **hooks and suckers** | Planaria (free-living), liver fluke, tapeworm |
| **Nemathelminthes** | Round, **unsegmented**, pointed at the ends | **False** (pseudocoelom) | Separate sexes; many parasites | Ascaris, hookworm, filarial worm |
| **Annelida** | Long, divided into **rings (segments)** | **True** cavity (coelom) | Bristles; moist skin | Earthworm, leech, Nereis |

A **coelom** is a body cavity completely lined by tissue; a false cavity is not fully lined.

key_terms.definition_md: A true body cavity, lined all round by tissue.
An organism that lives on or in another and takes food from it.
Having a body divided into repeated rings or parts.

sections.heading: 4. Arthropoda, Mollusca and Echinodermata
sections.body_md:
**Arthropoda** — the largest phylum: a **segmented body**, **jointed legs** and a hard outer skeleton (exoskeleton) that is moulted as the animal grows. Insects have **three body regions** (head, thorax, abdomen) and **three pairs of legs**; spiders have **four pairs** of legs. Examples: cockroach, butterfly, prawn, crab, spider, scorpion, centipede.

**Mollusca** — **soft, unsegmented body**, usually covered by a **mantle** that makes a **shell**, and a **muscular foot** for creeping. Examples: snail, mussel, octopus, cuttlefish (octopus and cuttlefish have no shell on the outside).

**Echinodermata** — **spiny skin**; **tube feet** for moving and catching food; body in five parts in adults; **all marine**. Examples: starfish, sea urchin, sea cucumber.

key_terms.definition_md: The hard outer covering of an arthropod.
A fold of skin of a mollusc that secretes the shell.
Small tube-like feet of an echinoderm used for movement.

sections.heading: 5. Chordates: Pisces and Amphibia
sections.body_md:
| Feature | Pisces (fishes) | Amphibia |
|---|---|---|
| Habitat | Water only | Land and water |
| Skin | **Scales** | **Moist, smooth**, no scales |
| Breathing | **Gills** | **Skin and lungs** (gills in the larva) |
| Limbs | **Fins** | Four limbs; webbed feet in many |
| Heart | **Two** chambers | **Three** chambers |
| Eggs | Laid in water | Laid in water; the larva (tadpole) changes by **metamorphosis** |
| Examples | Rohu, shark, seahorse | Frog, toad, salamander |

Both classes are **cold-blooded**: body temperature changes with the surroundings. Frogs lay eggs in water, so amphibians depend on water to breed.

key_terms.definition_md: A change of body form from the larva to the adult, as from tadpole to frog.
Having a body temperature that varies with the surroundings.

sections.heading: 6. Chordates: Reptilia, Aves and Mammalia
sections.body_md:
| Feature | Reptilia | Aves | Mammalia |
|---|---|---|---|
| Body covering | Dry **scales** | **Feathers** | **Hair** |
| Limbs | Four short legs (none in snakes) | Forelimbs form **wings** | Legs, wings (bat) or flippers (whale) |
| Heart | **Three** chambers | **Four** chambers | **Four** chambers |
| Body temperature | Cold-blooded | **Warm-blooded** | **Warm-blooded** |
| Young | Shelled eggs on **land** | Hard-shelled eggs | Born alive and fed with **milk** from **mammary glands** (most) |
| Other | Lungs; dry skin | **Beak**; **hollow bones**; lungs | External ear (pinna); **diaphragm** |
| Examples | Lizard, snake, turtle, crocodile | Crow, pigeon, penguin | Human, bat, whale, kangaroo |

To classify a vertebrate, work through the clues: gills and scales mean fish; moist skin and a larva mean amphibian; feathers mean bird; hair and mammary glands mean mammal; dry scales and shelled eggs on land mean reptile.

key_terms.definition_md: A gland of female mammals that makes milk to feed the young.
Keeping a constant body temperature whatever the surroundings.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing the phylum without a **feature** as reason.
- Calling a spider an insect, or an octopus an echinoderm; a spider is an **arthropod** with eight legs, an octopus is a **mollusc**.
- Putting a bat or a whale in the wrong class: both are **mammals**.
- Confusing a **false** body cavity (Nemathelminthes) with **no** cavity (Platyhelminthes) and a **true** cavity (Annelida).
- Writing four chambers for every reptile: most reptiles have **three** (the crocodile has four; books differ on how far it is taught).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: a term, an odd one out **with its category**, a reason.
- 2 marks: two features or two differences matched point for point.
- 3 marks: a table of three differences, or a neat, labelled diagram.
- 10-mark structured question: a short situation or diagram with parts of 3, 3 and 4 marks; one part is usually a labelled diagram.

questions.solution_md: Jointed legs and an exoskeleton are the marks of Arthropoda — option (c).

questions.solution_md: Amphibians have moist skin and a gilled larva — option (b).

questions.solution_md: Birds and mammals have two atria and two ventricles — option (c).

questions.solution_md: False. In chordates the nerve cord is hollow and lies on the back (dorsal) side.

questions.solution_md: Notochord.

questions.stem_md: State two differences between chordates and non-chordates.

answer.model_answer_md: Chordates have a **notochord** at some stage; non-chordates **have none**. The nerve cord of a chordate is **hollow and dorsal** (on the back); in a non-chordate it is **solid and ventral** (on the belly side).

questions.stem_md: Give reason: the phylum of sponges is named Porifera.

answer.model_answer_md: The name means **pore bearers**: the body of a sponge is full of **pores**.

questions.solution_md: Pore bearers.

questions.stem_md: Name the large opening and the small openings of a sponge, and state what passes through each.

answer.model_answer_md: The **pores** are the small openings; **water carrying food and oxygen** enters through them. The **osculum** is the large opening at the top; **water** leaves through it.

questions.solution_md: Pores in; osculum out.

questions.solution_md: Cnidoblasts; catch prey; jellyfish.

**Assertion (A):** An octopus belongs to the phylum Mollusca.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: The assertion is true. The reason is false: an octopus has a soft body and no outer shell — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A spider is an insect because it has jointed legs.
questions.solution_md: False. A spider is an arthropod, not an insect: it has eight legs and two body regions.

answer.model_answer_md: **Exoskeleton.**

questions.solution_md: Exoskeleton.

questions.stem_md: Five houseflies and two spiders rest on a window sill. A fly has 6 legs and a spider has 8 legs. How many legs are there in all?
questions.solution_md: Flies: $5 \times 6 = 30$; spiders: $2 \times 8 = 16$; total $= 46$.

questions.stem_md: State two features of echinoderms. Give one example.

answer.model_answer_md: Echinoderms have **spiny skin** and **tube feet** for movement (and are all **marine**, with a body in five parts in the adult). Example: **starfish** (sea urchin, sea cucumber).

questions.solution_md: Spiny skin; tube feet; starfish.

questions.stem_md: State two features of arthropods. Name two animals that are arthropods.

answer.model_answer_md: Arthropods have **jointed legs** and a hard outer skeleton (**exoskeleton**) with a segmented body. Examples: **cockroach** and **prawn** (also crab, spider, centipede).

questions.solution_md: Jointed legs; exoskeleton; two examples.

questions.stem_md: State three features of coelenterates. Name two examples.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. They live in water and the body is a **tube with two cell layers** around a central cavity.
2. A **single opening** is both mouth and anus, ringed by **tentacles**.
3. The tentacles carry **stinging cells (cnidoblasts)**.

Examples: **Hydra** and **jellyfish** (sea anemone, coral).

questions.solution_md: Two cell layers; tentacles and one opening; cnidoblasts; two examples.

marking_scheme.step: Two cell layers or tube body
Tentacles and single opening, or cnidoblasts

answer.model_answer_md: A body in **three regions**: a small **head** carrying a pair of **antennae**; a middle **thorax** bearing three pairs of jointed legs and a **wing**; and a longer segmented **abdomen**. Five labels with ruled lines.

questions.solution_md: Insect with three regions; five labels.

marking_scheme.step: Three body regions in the right order

questions.stem_md: Name the phylum of each of these animals and give one reason: (i) octopus, (ii) earthworm, (iii) sea urchin.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) Octopus: **Mollusca**: soft, unsegmented body with a mantle and muscular foot. (ii) Earthworm: **Annelida**: body divided into rings with a true cavity. (iii) Sea urchin: **Echinodermata**: spiny skin and tube feet.

questions.solution_md: Mollusca; Annelida; Echinodermata, each with a reason.

**Assertion (A):** Frogs are classified as reptiles.

**Reason (R):** Frogs have moist skin and lay their eggs in water.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

answer.model_answer_md: **Toad**; the others are **fishes (Pisces)**.

questions.solution_md: Toad is an amphibian.

questions.stem_md: Give the biological term: the change of a larva into an adult of a different body form, as in a tadpole.

answer.model_answer_md: **Metamorphosis.**

questions.solution_md: Metamorphosis.

questions.stem_md: Why must a frog return to water to breed? Name the process by which a tadpole becomes a frog.

answer.model_answer_md: A frog **lays its eggs in water**, and the tadpole is a **water-living larva with gills**, so it needs water to breed. The tadpole becomes a frog by **metamorphosis**.

questions.solution_md: Eggs and larva in water; metamorphosis.

questions.stem_md: Tabulate three differences between Pisces and Amphibia.

answer.model_answer_md:

|---|---|
| Live in **water only** | Live on **land and in water** |
| Skin has **scales** | Skin is **moist and smooth**, without scales |
| Breathe by **gills** | Breathe by **skin and lungs** |
| Heart has **two** chambers | Heart has **three** chambers |

questions.solution_md: Habitat; skin; breathing; heart.

questions.stem_md: A gardener finds a leathery-shelled egg buried in warm soil. The adult that laid it has dry scales and a three-chambered heart. It belongs to

questions.stem_md: A penguin cannot fly and swims in the sea, yet it is placed in the class Aves. The feature that places it there is that it

has feathers and lays hard-shelled eggs

questions.solution_md: Feathers and hard-shelled eggs are features of birds — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A whale lives in the sea and has flippers, but it breathes with lungs, has a four-chambered heart and feeds its young on milk. It is a
questions.solution_md: Lungs, a four-chambered heart and milk for the young mark a mammal — option (d).

questions.stem_md: On a cold morning, a lizard is sluggish while a crow is active. The reason is that

options.text_md: the crow has a three-chambered heart and the lizard a four-chambered heart
the lizard has feathers and the crow has scales
the crow breathes by gills and the lizard by lungs
the body temperature of the crow stays constant, but that of the lizard changes with the surroundings

questions.solution_md: Birds are warm-blooded, and reptiles are cold-blooded — option (d).

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but flying does not make an animal a mammal; hair and mammary glands do — option (d).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A whale feeds its young on milk made in mammary glands.
questions.solution_md: True. A whale is a mammal.

questions.stem_md: Give reason: a whale is not a fish although it lives in water.

answer.model_answer_md: A whale has **lungs**, **hair** (a few bristles), a **four-chambered heart** and **mammary glands**: it is a **mammal**.

questions.solution_md: It has mammalian features.

questions.stem_md: A shelf holds 30 vertebrate specimens: 9 fishes, 6 amphibians, 7 reptiles, 5 birds and 3 mammals. How many are warm-blooded?
questions.solution_md: Warm-blooded classes are Aves and Mammalia: $5 + 3 = 8$.

questions.stem_md: A bat flies, yet it is classified as a mammal. State two features that support this.

answer.model_answer_md: A bat has **hair** on its body and **mammary glands** that feed its young on **milk**. (It also has a four-chambered heart, an external ear and a diaphragm.)

questions.solution_md: Hair; mammary glands.

questions.stem_md: State three features of birds that help them to fly.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The **forelimbs are modified into wings**.
2. The body is covered with **light feathers**.
3. The bones are **hollow**, which makes the body light (and the **beak** is light too).

questions.solution_md: Wings; feathers; hollow bones.

questions.stem_md: Tabulate three differences between Aves and Mammalia.

| Have a **beak**, no mammary glands | Have **mammary glands** and an external ear |

questions.solution_md: Covering; limbs; young; beak or glands.

(b) Calculate the percentage of arthropods among the animals collected, and the number of molluscs and annelids together. [2]

(d) Draw a neat, labelled diagram of animal P, naming four parts. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** P: **Coelenterata**; Q: **Mollusca**; R: **Annelida**.

**(b)** Arthropods = 16 ÷ 40 × 100 = **40 percent**. Molluscs and annelids = 10 + 4 = **14**.

**(c)** **Jointed legs** and a hard outer skeleton (**exoskeleton**); a segmented body.

**(d)** A tube-shaped body with a **mouth** at the top surrounded by **tentacles**, a **basal disc** at the bottom, and a body wall with two layers (a **bud** may be shown). Four labels with ruled lines.

questions.solution_md: Coelenterata, Mollusca, Annelida; 40 percent and 14; jointed legs and exoskeleton; labelled Hydra.

questions.stem_md:
A student keeps a tray of specimens that holds 9 beetles and 4 scorpions. A beetle has 6 legs and a scorpion has 8 legs.

(a) Calculate the total number of legs on the animals in the tray. [2]

(b) Name the phylum to which both animals belong and state two features that show this. [3]

(c) State two ways in which a beetle differs from a scorpion in its body. [2]

(d) Draw a neat, labelled diagram of an insect, naming five parts. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Beetle legs = 9 × 6 = 54; scorpion legs = 4 × 8 = 32; total = **86**.

**(b)** **Arthropoda**: **jointed legs** and a hard outer skeleton (**exoskeleton**), with a segmented body.

**(c)** A beetle has **six legs** and **three body regions** (and antennae and wings); a scorpion has **eight legs** and **two body regions**, with no antennae or wings.

**(d)** A body in three regions: **head** with **antenna**, **thorax** with three pairs of legs and a **wing**, and a segmented **abdomen**. Five labels.

questions.solution_md: 86 legs; Arthropoda with two features; legs and body regions differ; labelled insect.

questions.stem_md:
Three worms are cut across and studied under a lens. Worm X has solid tissue between its body wall and its gut. Worm Y has a cavity between its body wall and its gut, but the cavity is not lined all round. Worm Z has a cavity lined all round, and its body is made of many rings.

(a) State the kind of body cavity of X, Y and Z. [3]

(b) Name the phylum of each worm. [3]

(c) Give one example each of worm X and worm Y. [2]

(d) Draw a neat, labelled diagram of the cross-section of worm Z, showing the body wall, the cavity and the gut. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** X: **no body cavity**; Y: **false body cavity**; Z: **true body cavity (coelom)**.

**(b)** X: **Platyhelminthes**; Y: **Nemathelminthes**; Z: **Annelida**.

**(c)** X: **tapeworm** (liver fluke, Planaria); Y: **Ascaris** (hookworm, filarial worm).

**(d)** A circle for the **body wall**; inside it a **coelom** lined all round; at the centre the **gut**. Three labels.

questions.solution_md: None, false, true cavity; Platyhelminthes, Nemathelminthes, Annelida; tapeworm and Ascaris; labelled cross-section.

marking_scheme.step: Cross-section with body wall, cavity and gut drawn and labelled

questions.stem_md:
The hearts of four vertebrates are studied. P has one atrium and one ventricle. Q has two atria and one ventricle. R has two atria and two ventricles, and the animal lays hard-shelled eggs. S has two atria and two ventricles, and the young are fed on milk.

(a) State the number of chambers in the heart of P and Q, and of R and S. [2]

(b) Name the class of R and the class of S. [2]

(c) Name the two classes that could have the heart of Q and state one feature that separates them. [3]

(d) Draw neat, labelled block diagrams of the hearts of P and S, naming the atrium and ventricle. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** P has **two** chambers and Q has **three**; R and S each have **four**.

**(b)** R: **Aves**; S: **Mammalia**.

**(c)** **Amphibia** and **Reptilia**. Amphibians have **moist skin and a gilled larva**; reptiles have **dry scales** and lay shelled eggs on land.

**(d)** P: one **atrium** block above one **ventricle** block. S: two **atria** blocks above two **ventricle** blocks. All blocks labelled.

questions.solution_md: Two, three, four, four; Aves and Mammalia; Amphibia and Reptilia with a separating feature; block diagrams.

marking_scheme.step: Block diagram of S with labels

questions.stem_md:
A museum label card was lost for four animals. W lives in the sea, has spiny skin and five arms. X flies at night, is warm-blooded and has hair and mammary glands. Y lives only in water and has scales, fins, gills and a two-chambered heart. Z has no legs, dry scaly skin and lays leathery-shelled eggs on land.

(a) Name the phylum or class of W, X, Y and Z. [4]

(b) A student says that X is a bird because it flies. State two reasons to show that the student is wrong. [2]

(c) Z has no legs. Give two features that show that Z is a chordate and not a worm. [2]

(d) Draw a neat outline of Y and label the fins, the tail, the gill region and the scales. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** W: **Echinodermata**; X: **Mammalia**; Y: **Pisces**; Z: **Reptilia**.

**(b)** X has **hair** and **mammary glands** (it feeds its young on milk); birds have **feathers** and lay **hard-shelled eggs**.

**(c)** Any two: Z has a **notochord (backbone)**, a **dorsal hollow nerve cord**, **gill slits at some stage** (embryo), a heart on the belly side.

**(d)** A streamlined fish body with **fins**, a **tail**, a **gill cover** and **scales**. Four labels.

questions.solution_md: Echinodermata, Mammalia, Pisces, Reptilia; hair and mammary glands; notochord and dorsal nerve cord; labelled fish.

questions.stem_md:
A shelf holds 30 vertebrate specimens: 9 fishes, 6 amphibians, 7 reptiles, 5 birds and 3 mammals.

(a) Calculate the number of cold-blooded specimens and their percentage of all the specimens, correct to one decimal place. [3]

(b) Name the warm-blooded classes and state the number of heart chambers in them. [2]

(c) State two differences between amphibians and reptiles. [2]

(d) Draw a neat, labelled diagram of a frog, naming four parts. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Cold-blooded = 9 + 6 + 7 = **22**; percentage = 22 ÷ 30 × 100 = **73.3 percent**.

**(b)** **Aves** and **Mammalia**; each has **four** chambers.

**(c)** Amphibians have **moist skin** and lay eggs **in water** (larva with gills); reptiles have **dry scales** and lay **shelled eggs on land**. (Amphibians have a larval stage and metamorphosis.)

**(d)** A frog with a broad **head**, **eyes**, **nostrils**, short **forelimbs** and long **hind limbs** with **webbed feet**. Four labels.

questions.solution_md: 22 cold-blooded, 73.3 percent; Aves and Mammalia with four chambers; skin and eggs differ; labelled frog.

questions.stem_md:
On a rocky shore a boy finds a starfish, a snail and an octopus in a rock pool.

(a) Name the phylum of each of the three animals. [2]

(b) The octopus has no shell. State two features that show that it is closely related to the snail. [2]

(c) Tabulate three differences between the starfish and the snail. [3]

(d) Draw a neat, labelled diagram of the starfish, seen from above, naming three parts. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Starfish: **Echinodermata**; snail and octopus: **Mollusca**.

**(b)** Both have a **soft, unsegmented body** with a **mantle**, and a **muscular foot** (modified into arms in the octopus).

**(c)**

| Starfish | Snail |
|---|---|
| **Spiny** skin | **Soft** body with a mantle |
| Moves on **tube feet** | Moves on a **muscular foot** |
| Body in **five parts**, no shell | Usually a **coiled shell** |

**(d)** A star with **five arms** and a central **disc**; **tube feet** along the arms and the **mouth** on the underside. Three labels.

questions.solution_md: Echinodermata and Mollusca; soft body with mantle and foot; three differences; labelled starfish.

questions.stem_md: A student has pictures of a leech, a sea urchin, a toad and Hydra. Which one is a vertebrate?
questions.solution_md: The toad is an amphibian, a chordate with a backbone; the other three are non-chordates — option (d).

questions.stem_md: What is a notochord? State what replaces it in a vertebrate.

answer.model_answer_md: A **notochord** is a **stiff supporting rod along the back** of a chordate. In a vertebrate it is **replaced by the backbone** (vertebral column) as the animal grows.

questions.solution_md: Rod along the back; replaced by the backbone.

questions.stem_md: State two features of a fish that help it to live in water.

answer.model_answer_md: A fish has **gills** to take oxygen from the water, and **fins** and a **streamlined body** (with a slimy, scaly skin) for swimming.

questions.solution_md: Gills; fins and streamlined body.
